clinical_pearls: Calcific aortic stenosis is a common cause of acquired complete heart block in the elderly due to calcium extension from the aortic annulus into the adjacent His bundle and bundle branches
Cardiac syncope is characterized by sudden onset without prodrome and rapid full recovery without post-ictal confusion
Complete heart block is a Class I indication for permanent pacemaker implantation regardless of symptoms
Syncope in the setting of moderate-to-severe aortic stenosis is a Class I indication for aortic valve intervention
Prolonged QTc in the setting of bradycardia increases the risk of pause-dependent torsades de pointes

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Ryo Nakamura is an 82-year-old man with a significant cardiac history including moderate aortic stenosis, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and chronic kidney disease who presents to the emergency department via ambulance after his daughter found him unresponsive on the hallway floor of his apartment at approximately 6:45 AM. According to the patient and his daughter, he had gotten out of bed and was walking to the bathroom when he suddenly felt a brief sensation of the room going dark, followed immediately by loss of consciousness. He fell forward, striking the right side of his head on the wall. His daughter, who had arrived early to check on him, heard the thud and found him lying on the floor. She estimates he was unresponsive for approximately 15 to 20 seconds. She reports that she did not witness any shaking, jerking, or stiffening of the limbs. There was no foaming at the mouth, no tongue biting, and no urinary or fecal incontinence. Upon regaining consciousness, Mr. Nakamura was immediately lucid and coherent, asking his daughter why she was on the floor next to him. There was no period of confusion or disorientation. He reports a dull headache from striking the wall but denies any chest pain, shortness of breath, or palpitations before or after the event. Over the past two to three months, he has experienced four or five episodes of sudden lightheadedness lasting a few seconds each, sometimes accompanied by a sensation that his vision was graying out. These occurred at various times of day and in different positions, including while seated. He stopped his daily walks because of increasing fatigue and a fear of collapsing outside. He denies any prior seizures, and he has never had an episode of loss of consciousness before the recent cluster. He has not experienced any fever, weight loss, or night sweats. His daughter confirms he has been taking all his medications regularly and has not started any new drugs recently.
